title: Orpheus and Eurydice
subtitle: The love that defies death
subject: mythologie
description: Orpheus goes down to the underworld to bring Eurydice back. His music bends death itself. One forbidden glance is enough to lose everything.

hero.hook: His lyre calms the underworld. His doubt hands Eurydice back to it forever.

blocks.text: **Orpheus** was a musician whose lyre could move even stones. When his wife **Eurydice** died, he refused to mourn. He went down alive among the dead to bring her back.
The Latin poets [[Virgil]] and [[Ovid]] fixed the story in its classic form. Beyond the tragic love, it is a tale about doubt, impatience, and the power of art against death.

Orpheus was the son of the Muse **Calliope**. His **lyre**, a gift from **Apollo**, god of the arts, was not there only to please an audience. It soothed wild animals, moved trees, and calmed savage nature. Where other heroes won by force, Orpheus won by harmony.

blocks.caption: Orpheus and his lyre, art as power over the world

blocks.text: During the expedition of the **Argonauts**, led by the hero [[Jason]], the Sirens tried to lure the crew. Orpheus sang louder and saved his companions. Then he married the dryad **Eurydice**, a nymph of the woods. The happiness was brief.
On her wedding day, Eurydice fled the shepherd [[Aristaeus]]. She stepped on a snake. The venom killed her. Her shade set off for the [[Styx]], the river of the underworld.

sections.title: Going down alive among the dead

blocks.text: Orpheus attempted a [[catabasis]], a descent into the underworld. No weapons. Only his music. It put [[Cerberus]] to sleep, the three-headed dog that guards the entrance. It won over [[Charon]], the ferryman of the dead.

Before **Hades** and **Persephone**, rulers of the world below, Orpheus played the most devastating tune of his life. The underworld stopped for a moment. **Sisyphus** and **Tantalus** forgot their torment. The [[Erinyes]], goddesses of vengeance, wept.
In some versions, Orpheus moved Persephone by reminding her of her own abduction by Hades. The queen of the dead recognized his grief.
Hades granted the impossible: Eurydice could go back up. But there was one absolute condition. Orpheus had to walk ahead of her without looking back until they reached the light.
The climb back was agony. Behind him, silence. Shades make no sound. Near the exit, doubt won. What if Hades had tricked him? Orpheus **turned around**.
Their eyes met for a second. Then the darkness snatched Eurydice away. This time the loss came from a human mistake. The passage closed. Orpheus wandered, then withdrew to Thrace.

After his death, the head of Orpheus was thrown into the river [[Hebrus]] and supposedly drifted all the way to Lesbos. There it is said to have become an oracle so powerful that **Apollo** himself demanded its silence.
His refusal of any new love enraged the [[Maenads]], priestesses of **Dionysus** caught in a ritual frenzy. They tore him apart. His lyre kept singing anyway, carried off by the current.
Out of the death of Orpheus came [[Orphism]], a religious movement that promised salvation of the soul through rites of purification. Death was no longer a dull ending, but a crossing to prepare for.

The “glance of Orpheus” still inspires opera, film, notably in the work of [[Jean Cocteau]], and literature. For [[Maurice Blanchot]], the artist is the one who looks into the darkness, even at the cost of losing what he loves. In the end the gods set the lyre in the sky as a constellation: art lasts longer than the artist.
**Orpheus** charmed the underworld with his music, then lost **Eurydice** by turning around too soon. Art can bend death. Human doubt gets the last word.
